name: HEAR
ability_definition: The ability to detect or tell the differences between sounds that vary in pitch and loudness.

task_realism.reasoning: NSynth Pitch asks the system to label isolated, clean instrument notes with one of 88 pitches. Pitch discrimination is part of Hearing Sensitivity, and the task is realistic for jobs like piano tuning or music work. Most workplace uses are different, though. They involve noticing a change in machine pitch, hearing a faint alarm, telling an abnormal engine or equipment sound from a normal one, or hearing threshold tones in audiology. Those tasks involve real acoustic scenes, not single synthesized notes.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Stimuli are clean, studio-quality, single-note clips from NSynth, with no background noise, reverberation or competing sources. Evaluation freezes the embeddings and trains a shallow classifier on 5h or 50h of labeled in-distribution data. Real work requires detecting and discriminating sounds in noisy, variable environments without task-specific supervised calibration. There is also no graded-difficulty or threshold protocol.

construct_coverage.reasoning: The benchmark covers only pitch identification (pitch and chroma accuracy). The loudness half of the definition is absent. So is detection sensitivity, meaning whether a faint sound is present at all. It does not measure just-noticeable differences either: 88-class semitone labeling is coarse compared with the fine pitch differences the ability involves. At best this is a narrow slice of one of the ability's two dimensions.

format_match.reasoning: The input is real audio, which fits the modality. The output is a forced 88-way categorical label, not a same/different judgment, a detection report or an 'is this sound abnormal' decision. Pitch naming is a genuine artifact in musical work but is artificial for most occupational listening tasks.

transferability_reasoning: HEAR's NSynth Pitch task tests pitch classification of clean, isolated instrument notes under a frozen-embedding, supervised-probe protocol. It says little about detecting or discriminating sounds in real noisy work settings. It omits loudness discrimination and detection thresholds entirely, and it is coarser than true fine-grained discrimination, so transfer to the full Hearing Sensitivity ability is weak.

2022.human_reference: Workers whose jobs rely on hearing sensitivity, such as musicians, audio technicians and sound engineers, with the general adult workforce as the broader frame.
